segments.say: And now, let's go back, very slowly, to the garden where the street party was. The tables are gone. The people have all gone home. What's left is just the garden, in the middle of the night, with the last of the lanterns glowing on the fence and a soft scatter of fireflies in the hedge.

Everything is quiet. The grass is cool and a little damp. The air smells of cut lawn and honeysuckle. Somewhere beyond the fence, a cat steps along a wall without a sound. It's a completely different garden from the one that was full of voices only hours ago, and a very kind one, because it asks nothing of you.

Here's the garden as it is now. A few hanging lanterns, still faintly glowing. Fireflies drifting like slow, tiny stars among the leaves. Above it all, a sky full of faint stars, soft and silver against the deep blue. There are no faces here, and no names, and nothing to recognise or to recall. Just a garden at night, doing what gardens do.

Watch the lanterns on the fence, going out, one by one. Each one gives a last small flicker and then fades to a warm, dim glow, and then to dark. The garden grows a little darker with each, and a little calmer. It's the gentlest kind of ending, each light letting go in its own time, and none of them in any hurry at all.

Now let tonight's places begin to fade, one by one, like lamps being turned down in a long hallway. The window with its quiet rain. The night train, rocking through the fields. The pond, with its fireflies. The misty valley, steaming softly. The warm kitchen, with its lantern. Everything is growing quiet, and slow, and soft.

Take one more slow breath now. In, through the nose, gently. And out, long and easy, letting everything go. Feel how heavy and warm your body is. Feel how calm and slow your breath has become. There's nothing left to do tonight. The day is done, the night is kind, and rest is already on its way.

And in her quiet house, Marta is nearly asleep. The rain has stopped. Her breathing is long and slow. And somewhere, in that soft, hazy place between waking and dreaming, a name floats up, quite by itself, the way a leaf rises to the surface of a pond. Anselm, she thinks. His name was Anselm. And she smiles, and she's asleep before she can be sure.

Sometimes the name comes when you stop looking. We can't promise that it always will, or say exactly why it does when it does. But the mind does keep working on the things that matter to it, even when we've stopped asking. And if it doesn't come tonight, there's always the morning, and a friendly hello, and a kind admission.

show.text: Sometimes the name comes when you stop looking.

segments.say: Thank you for spending this quiet evening here. I hope you feel a little lighter, and a little kinder towards your own memory, and a little more curious about the small, quiet ways our minds work. Let your breath be slow. Let your body be heavy. Let your dreams wander wherever they like, over night trains, and lily ponds, and warm kitchens. Sleep softly, and rest well. The night is long, and it is gentle, and you are safe in it. Let it hold you, from the top of your head to the tips of your toes, until morning comes by itself.

On top of the garden wall, a cat is walking, slowly, with its tail held high. It pauses, looks at the garden for a long moment, and then steps on, unhurried, into the dark. It knows every wall and fence on the street, and it has never needed a single name to find its way. There's something deeply restful about an animal that goes through the night so gently.

Look up now at the stars, so many and so quiet. Each one is a long way off, older than any name anyone ever gave it, and they've been shining on gardens like this one for longer than anyone has been counting. They ask nothing. They just shine, and you're lying under them, small and warm and entirely welcome.

Wherever you are tonight, whether in a quiet bedroom or a crowded house or a room that isn't your own, you can carry this garden with you. The lanterns, the fireflies, the cool grass, the stars. They'll be here whenever you want them. All you need to do is close your eyes, take one slow breath, and you're back among them.

Somewhere in the hedge, honeysuckle is flowering, and its sweet smell drifts through the night air in slow, warm waves. Breathe it in, if you can imagine it, and let it settle in your chest. It's the smell of long evenings, of open windows, of summers that seemed to last forever. It asks nothing of you, and it gives you a great deal.

Let your breaths come very slowly now, one by one, each one a little longer than the last. In the garden, the last firefly is blinking out. The last lantern is fading. The last of the day is dissolving into the dark, and you're dissolving with it, gently, warmly, without any fear.

And next time, if you'd like to join me again, we'll explore another very human puzzle. How we seem to decide what a stranger is like in the first few seconds of meeting them, and what science says about whether we're right. We'll look at it gently, and without any blame. Until then, rest well. Goodnight.
